title: The heavens shew forth (Psalm 18 [19])
hookLine: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey

cards: A sunset over a highway. A driver pulls onto the shoulder and holds up a phone, and the picture comes out flat. The phone goes back in a pocket, and the driver just looks.

There aren't any words. And yet it's as if something has been said. A poet in ancient Israel had that same feeling and wrote it down, then did something unexpected: he put the sky and a book side by side.

teach.b: Psalm 18 in the Douay, 19 in most Bibles, opens: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." Shew is the old spelling of show.
The firmament is the great dome of the sky; the Hebrew word pictures something hammered flat, like beaten metal. Then: "Day to day uttereth speech, and night to night sheweth knowledge."
Each day hands the news to the next, like a relay. And yet: "There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard." The sky speaks in no language, so everyone on earth can hear it.

teach.h: THE SUN RUNS LIKE A BRIDEGROOM.
teach.b: The sun comes out each morning like a bridegroom from his chamber, rejoicing like a giant to run his way, nothing hidden from its heat.
Then, halfway through, the psalm turns to the law of the Lord, God's teaching: it converts souls, gives wisdom to little ones, rejoices hearts.
The commandments are "more to be desired than gold and many precious stones: and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." Why put these together?
An old Christian image speaks of two books, creation and scripture. In that picture, the sky shows that there is glory, and the page names whose it is.
After both, the psalm ends small and personal, asking to be cleansed of hidden faults, and that the words of the mouth and the thoughts of the heart would be pleasing.
This week went from the saints' calendar to a rule of life to the first psalms. Here the sky and the page meet.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 18 [19] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear its second half at Mass, often as the responsorial psalm answering a reading about God's law.

games.q: the psalm has just praised the sky and the sun. what does it turn to next?
o: the law of the Lord, sweeter than honey.
games.why: it turns to God's law, more to be desired than gold. creation and scripture, side by side.

practice: Go to a window or step outside and look up for a minute; if you can't, close your eyes and remember a sky you've seen. Don't describe it: notice the light, the color, how far it goes, and let it speak without words.
If you pray, end with the psalm's first line, the heavens shew forth the glory of God; if you don't, let the sky be enough.

wordCard.voice: Firmament. The great dome of the sky, pictured as something hammered flat, the sky that speaks God's glory without a word. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the heavens are telling. the verb is related to the word for counting and recounting a story.

carryVoice: Your line: the sky is preaching. It just doesn't use words. Day one hundred sixty-one, done.
